sentences.text: The genus name Phuwiangvenator combines the Phu Wiang mountains where it was found and the Latin word for hunter, while the species name yaemniyomi honors Sudham Yaemniyom, a Thai paleontologist who first discovered fossils in the region. This animal is the only known species in its genus, P. yaemniyomi. The holotype specimen was discovered in 1993 in Thailand's Khon Kaen province by a team led by Preecha Sainongkham.

Researchers estimate that Phuwiangvenator was approximately 6 meters long in life. The preserved dorsal vertebra has an hourglass shape when viewed from above, similar to other avetheropods. Phuwiangvenator is distinguished from Siamotyrannus by having dorsal vertebrae that are longer than they are tall.
The three preserved sacral vertebrae are fused together and were significantly damaged during fossilization. Phuwiangvenator has less convex rims on its sacral centra compared to Siamotyrannus.
Phuwiangvenator had only one groove on the body of the astragalus, unlike Vayuraptor which had two.

A metatarsal of the Phuwiangvenator holotype showed signs of a greenstick fracture, analyzed by Samathi and colleagues in 2022. The texture of the fractured bone suggests the fracture healed, implying the animal survived the injury. Computer tomography of the bone led authors to conclude the animal was not fully grown when it died.

The holotype specimen was found in 1993 and named and described scientifically in 2019. Fossils were found in rocks of the Sao Khua Formation in Thailand. The Sao Khua Formation contains the most abundant and diverse Mesozoic fossils in northeastern Thailand.

In other megaraptorans, furrows on the first claw are thought to be attachment sites for powerful muscles that enabled greater control and flexibility of finger movements. Phuwiangvenator did not possess the same specialized arm musculature for feeding as other megaraptorans.
Researchers conclude the most likely cause of the fracture was the animal hitting its foot on a hard object or falling over.
Some authors suggest the healed fracture implies herding behavior, though others propose the animal simply survived with a limp.
Phuwiangvenator is classified within the unranked family Megaraptora. Phylogenetic analyses found Phuwiangvenator to be the most basal megaraptoran.
In the original phylogenetic analysis, Phuwiangvenator was recovered as a basal member of Megaraptora alongside Siamotyrannus.

Phuwiangvenator lived during the Early Cretaceous period, approximately 125 to 120 million years ago. This extinct megaraptoran theropod lived in what is now Thailand during the Early Cretaceous. Phuwiangvenator lived during the Early Cretaceous, approximately 130 million years ago in the Barremian stage. The animal lived in what is now Asia. The time range for Phuwiangvenator is from 125.77 to 121.4 million years ago.

The Sao Khua Formation sediments indicate a fluvial environment that included lakes, floodplains, and braided channels. Reports of ichthyosaur and plesiosaur teeth from the Sao Khua Formation have been reidentified as belonging to non-marine crocodyliformes.

Describers suggest that the discovery of Phuwiangvenator in Thailand supports an Asian origin for megaraptorans. A 2024 analysis by Andrea Cau placed Phuwiangvenator within the family Coeluridae, differing from earlier classifications. Recent studies have debated the classification of Phuwiangvenator, with some analyses placing it in the family Coeluridae.
